units.title: Unit 03 — Using your dictionary
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 10–11 (PDF pages 14–15).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Learning about collocations · dictionary use and lexical partners
learningObjectives: Use learner’s dictionaries to identify natural word combinations and their register.
Distinguish collocations that cause, describe or relieve physical pain.
Use authentic patterns with uncountable advice, and express accepting an offer in different registers.
Notice differences in strength and meaning among related pain expressions.

items.example: If you find an unfamiliar term, look up a word before continuing.
items.note: Look up means search for a word or expression in a dictionary, usually to check meaning, spelling or usage.

items.example: The cyclist was in pain after falling off his bike.
items.note: Use be in pain to describe someone experiencing physical pain; the noun is uncountable here.

items.example: She has had constant pain in her shoulder for several weeks.
items.note: Constant indicates pain that continues rather than appearing only occasionally.

items.example: The doctor asked whether the patient had abdominal pain.
items.note: Abdominal is the medical adjective for the area around the stomach and intestines.

items.example: A warm compress may help ease the pain in his back.
items.note: Ease the pain means reduce how strongly pain is felt, not necessarily remove it completely.

items.pt: uma dor aguda; uma dor forte e súbita
items.example: She felt a sharp pain in her ankle while running.
items.note: Sharp describes a sudden, intense or piercing sensation; compare a dull ache.

items.example: After the hike, we all complained about our aches and pains.
items.note: A familiar plural expression for various minor or recurring bodily pains.

items.pt: um incômodo; uma pessoa ou coisa irritante
items.example: Filling in the same form twice is a real pain in the neck.
items.note: An informal idiom for an annoying person or situation, not usually a literal neck injury.

items.example: A poorly fitting shoe can cause pain after a long walk.
items.note: Cause describes producing pain; unlike relieve pain, it indicates the source of suffering.

items.example: The investigation examined whether the guards had deliberately inflicted pain.
items.note: Inflict is used for intentionally imposing physical or emotional suffering; stronger and more formal than cause.

items.example: Several patients began to complain of pain after the procedure.
items.note: In medical descriptions, complain of pain reports a symptom; complain about pain is also possible in everyday speech.

items.example: Some people experience pain long after an injury has healed.
items.note: A neutral or relatively formal way to say feel pain, common in health information.

items.example: You may feel pain in your muscles after an intense workout.
items.note: Feel pain is the most straightforward everyday expression for sensing pain.

items.pt: estar tomado por dores intensas; sofrer dores lancinantes
items.example: He was racked with pain while waiting for medical help.
items.note: Racked with pain is a strong expression for severe suffering, not for a minor ache.

items.example: People with untreated injuries can suffer pain for a long time.
items.note: Suffer pain emphasises the unpleasant experience and can sound more formal than feel pain.

items.example: The treatment aims to alleviate pain and improve mobility.
items.note: Alleviate is a relatively formal verb for making pain less severe.

items.example: Changing his posture helped lessen pain in his lower back.
items.note: Lessen means decrease the degree of pain; it does not necessarily mean eliminate it.

items.example: The medicine is intended to relieve pain after surgery.
items.note: Relieve pain is a common healthcare expression for reducing physical discomfort.

items.pt: acalmar a dor; amenizar o desconforto
items.example: A cool cloth can soothe pain caused by mild sunburn.
items.note: Soothe suggests calming or gently easing discomfort.

items.pt: a dor diminui; a dor passa gradualmente
items.example: After a short rest, the pain subsides and he can walk again.
items.note: Subside means become weaker or less intense; the subject is pain, not the patient.

items.pt: uma dor surda; dor persistente e pouco intensa
items.example: I noticed a dull ache in my knees after sitting for hours.
items.note: A dull ache is usually less sharp and often more persistent than a sharp pain.

items.pt: estar com dor de barriga; estar com dor de estômago
items.example: I sometimes have a stomach ache after eating too quickly.
items.note: Ache is a countable noun in this expression; stomach ache may also be written stomachache.

items.example: Experienced colleagues often give advice to new employees.
items.note: Advice is uncountable in English; do not say an advice.

items.example: My supervisor gave me good advice about preparing for interviews.
items.note: Good advice is uncountable; its Portuguese translation may be singular or plural.

items.example: Can I offer you a piece of advice before the meeting?
items.note: Use a piece of advice to count an individual suggestion, not an advice.

items.example: I decided to take your advice and apply for the course.
items.note: Take advice means act on a recommendation; it does not mean physically receive an object.

items.example: The workshop provides practical advice on finding a job.
items.note: Advice on introduces the topic; about is also possible in many contexts.

items.example: Ask for expert advice before signing a complex contract.
items.note: Expert advice comes from a person with specialist knowledge.

items.example: The guide gives practical advice on managing a budget.
items.note: Practical focuses on useful steps that can be put into action.

items.example: She sought legal advice before replying to the complaint.
items.note: Legal advice is guidance about legal rights or obligations, commonly supplied by a qualified professional.

items.example: He chose to follow her advice and postpone the purchase.
items.note: Follow advice means do what was recommended; the possessive can change with the speaker.

items.pt: por conselho dela; seguindo a orientação dela
items.example: On her advice, we checked the figures once more.
items.note: On someone’s advice explains whose recommendation prompted an action.

items.pt: uma oferta gentil; um oferecimento generoso
items.example: Thank you for such a kind offer to help us move house.
items.note: Kind describes a considerate or generous offer, not necessarily a low price.

items.word: take you up on your offer
items.pt: aceitar sua oferta; aceitar seu oferecimento
items.example: I would love to take you up on your offer to drive me home.
items.note: An informal way to accept someone’s offer; the person and possessive can vary.

items.pt: aceitar uma oferta; aceitar uma proposta
items.example: She plans to accept an offer from a different employer.
items.note: A more neutral or formal alternative to take someone up on an offer.

units.title: Unit 04 — Types of collocation
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 12–13 (PDF pages 16–17).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Learning about collocations · grammatical combination patterns
learningObjectives: Identify adjective–noun, noun–verb, noun–noun, verb–preposition, verb–adverb and adverb–adjective collocations.
Choose natural verb partners for business and economic developments.
Express strong feelings with a surge of, a pang of, swell with and burst into.
Distinguish manner adverbs from intensifiers and observe their typical partners.

items.example: A bright colour can make a small room feel cheerful.
items.note: Bright describes a vivid or strong colour rather than a dark or muted one.

items.pt: uma conversa rápida; um bate-papo breve
items.example: We had a brief chat before the training session began.
items.note: Brief describes a conversation that lasts only a short time.

items.pt: um problema grave; um grande problema
items.example: Traffic congestion is a major problem in the city centre.
items.note: Major emphasises importance or seriousness, not merely physical size.

items.pt: uma questão central; um ponto fundamental
items.example: Cost is a key issue in the discussion about the new project.
items.note: Key identifies a matter that has particular importance for a decision or discussion.

items.pt: um fator decisivo; um fator importante
items.example: Reliable communication was a key factor in the team’s success.
items.note: A key factor is an important cause or element influencing an outcome.

items.example: A ginger cat was sleeping beside our front door.
items.note: Ginger is the usual British English adjective for the orange-brown colour of a cat’s fur.

items.pt: a economia cresce rapidamente; a economia vive um boom
items.example: When demand rises sharply, the economy booms and businesses hire more staff.
items.note: Boom means grow very strongly over a period, especially in economic contexts.

items.example: As a company grows, it often needs more experienced managers.
items.note: Grow describes an increase in business size or activity.

items.example: When a company expands, it may open offices in other cities.
items.note: Expand focuses on extending the scale, reach or operations of a business.

items.example: When two companies merge, their teams may need to share systems.
items.note: Merge describes organisations joining to form one business or group.

items.example: The startup hopes to launch a product before the end of the year.
items.note: Launch means officially introduce a product to the market, not physically throw it.

items.pt: representar um problema; criar uma dificuldade
items.example: Limited storage space could pose a problem for the new equipment.
items.note: Pose a problem means present or create a difficulty; do a problem is not a valid replacement.

items.example: Online courses can create opportunities for people in remote areas.
items.note: Create combines naturally with opportunities to describe possibilities that become available.

items.example: The team needs to make a decision before Friday.
items.note: Make is the conventional verb with decision; do a decision is not idiomatic.

items.pt: os preços sobem; os preços aumentam
items.example: When fuel prices rise, delivery costs often increase as well.
items.note: Rise is intransitive here: prices rise, but companies raise prices.

items.example: He felt a surge of anger when he discovered the deception.
items.note: A surge of anger is a sudden, strong increase in angry feeling; slightly literary.

items.example: The volunteers felt a sense of pride in their work.
items.note: A sense of pride is a feeling of satisfaction about an achievement or association.

items.pt: uma pontada de nostalgia; uma saudade repentina
items.example: The old photograph brought a pang of nostalgia.
items.note: Pang suggests a brief, sharp feeling; nostalgia concerns the past.

items.example: A surge of emotion caught her by surprise at the ceremony.
items.note: The pattern a surge of plus a feeling describes a powerful, sudden emotional response.

items.example: His grandparents swelled with pride at the graduation ceremony.
items.note: Swell with pride means feel visibly or deeply proud.

items.pt: ficar horrorizado; ser tomado pelo horror
items.example: The witnesses were filled with horror by what they saw.
items.note: Filled with horror expresses an intense feeling of fear or shock.

items.pt: cair no choro; começar a chorar de repente
items.example: She burst into tears when she heard the sad news.
items.note: Burst into tears means begin crying suddenly; into is required.

items.example: The audience began to roar with laughter at the comedian’s joke.
items.note: Roar with laughter conveys very loud, enthusiastic laughing.

items.example: At the end of the celebration, everyone burst into song.
items.note: Burst into song means suddenly start singing; it is not the same as burst into tears.

items.example: The worker had to pull steadily to lift the heavy crate.
items.note: Steadily describes a firm, even action without sudden changes.

items.example: Please place the glass gently on the shelf.
items.note: Gently describes a careful action done without force.

items.pt: sussurrar baixinho; falar em voz muito baixa
items.example: He leaned closer to whisper softly during the performance.
items.note: Softly reinforces the quiet and gentle manner of whispering.

items.example: She smiled proudly after completing her first marathon.
items.note: Proudly tells us the feeling behind the smile, not how wide it is.

items.pt: pisar com cuidado; agir com cautela
items.example: You should tread carefully on the wet rocks by the river.
items.note: Tread carefully means walk cautiously; it can also mean act sensitively in a difficult situation.

items.pt: feliz no casamento; casado e feliz
items.example: They have been happily married for nearly twenty years.
items.note: Happily married refers to a satisfying marriage, not simply a wedding day.

items.example: The engineer is fully aware of the safety requirements.
items.note: Fully aware means knowing and understanding something completely; commonly followed by of or that.

items.pt: completamente alheio; sem a menor ideia
items.example: He was blissfully unaware of the surprise party.
items.note: Often ironic: the person does not realise something important, sometimes unpleasant.

items.example: After their holiday, they seemed blissfully happy.
items.note: Blissfully intensifies happiness; unlike blissfully unaware, it directly describes pleasure.

items.example: Forgetting the guest’s name was acutely embarrassing.
items.note: Acutely makes the embarrassment sound especially intense; very embarrassing is less emphatic.
